concepts.short: Deeper plain networks have higher training error than shallower ones, even though the deeper model's solution space contains the shallower one's; this is the core challenge the paper addresses.
Instead of learning H(x) directly, a few stacked layers learn F(x) = H(x) - x, and the original mapping becomes F(x) + x via a shortcut connection.
A connection that skips one or more layers by adding the original input x to the output of the stacked layers, F(x); uses no extra parameters.
A three-layer block (1x1, 3x3, 1x1 convolution) used for deeper ResNets (50+ layers), where the 1x1 layers reduce and restore dimensions to make the 3x3 layer a low-dimensional bottleneck.
A standard convolutional neural network — the baseline in this paper — that stacks Conv/BN/ReLU layers without shortcut connections, used as a comparison to show the degradation problem.
A shortcut connection that uses a learned linear projection (usually a 1x1 convolution) to match dimensions when input and output sizes differ; an alternative to zero-padding.
A technique that normalizes each layer's activations across a mini-batch, used in all models to enable convergence and avoid vanishing/exploding gradients.
In the degradation problem, if identity were optimal, a stack of nonlinear layers should learn to compute F(x)=0; residual learning makes this easy by driving weights toward zero.
Using bottleneck blocks reduces the time complexity per layer compared to two 3x3 layers, allowing very deep networks (e.g., 152 layers) with lower total FLOPs than VGG-19.
